task.title: Priorities should be configurable per project like Status
task.description:
Make task priorities configurable per project, with the same machinery statuses
already have. Approved design; implement as three stacked PRs.

## Decisions

1. FULL PARITY with the status vocabulary: add, rename (with forwarding),
   remove/retire (with forwarding), reorder, relabel, and a `default` tag
   replacing the hardcoded medium.
2. PER-PRIORITY COLOR in config, `#rrggbb`, optional, with a position-derived
   ramp as the fallback when unset.
3. THREE STACKED PRs, one spec. Stage 1 is invisible to users.
4. SHARED PRIMITIVES, TWO TYPED FACADES (approach C): the kind-agnostic half of
   vocabulary.go becomes unexported generics over ~string; Vocabulary and
   PriorityVocabulary stay separate exported types.

## Data model

A third section in ConfigData, following the display precedent exactly. Nil
means the built-in low/medium/high, so every checkpoint written before this
section encodes to exactly the bytes it was stored as.

    type ConfigData struct {
        Vocabulary VocabularyDocument `json:"vocabulary"`
        Display    *DisplayDocument   `json:"display,omitempty"`
        Priorities *PriorityDocument  `json:"priorities,omitempty"`
    }

    type PriorityDocument struct {
        Priorities []PriorityDefinition `json:"priorities"` // by rank, then name
        Aliases    []PriorityAlias      `json:"aliases"`    // rename forwardings
        Retired    []RetiredPriority    `json:"retired"`    // removal forwardings
    }

    type PriorityDefinition struct {
        Priority Priority      `json:"priority"`
        Label    string        `json:"label"`
        Rank     string        `json:"rank"`            // reduced rational
        Tags     []PriorityTag `json:"tags"`            // only `default` today
        Color    string        `json:"color,omitempty"` // unset: derive from position
    }

Rank is a reduced-rational string, not an index, for the reason statuses use
one: two clones inserting a priority between the same two neighbours must not
have to coordinate. Most urgent sorts first, so `--before high` reads as "more
urgent than high".

core.Priority stays a string type so the ~128 existing references keep
compiling. What changes is that isValidPriority and priorityOrder stop
consulting a package-level array and start consulting the project's vocabulary,
with the zero value meaning "not configured, use built-in".

Tags is a list carrying one legal tag rather than a Default bool, chosen for
parity with statuses and to reuse the tag normalization primitive.

## What gets extracted (approach C)

Unexported generics over ~string:
  - forwarding chain resolution and forwardTerminates
  - AppendRank / InsertRank arithmetic
  - alias and retirement normalization
  - growth validation

Stays typed per kind:
  - status tags (default/next/done), IsNext, IsDone
  - priority tags (default only), Color
  - each type's Validate and its own arity invariants

The status refactor is pure extraction: vocabulary_test.go and
vocabulary_authoring_test.go must pass UNEDITED. That is the proof it changed
no meaning.

## Operations and compatibility

Eight operation types:

    priority.add      priority.rename    priority.relabel   priority.remove
    priority.reorder  priority.tag       priority.untag     priority.recolor

recolor is its own operation rather than a flag on relabel, because a color is
the one field that can be cleared back to the derived ramp - the same set/unset
shape display.set/display.unset has.

Compatibility costs a generation:
  - every priority.* op gets configOperationMinReader = 3
  - SupportedFormatGeneration goes 2 -> 3
  - ConfigPackMinReader gains the genesis guard display has, for
    operation.Config.Priorities != nil

The generation bump is the LAST commit of stage 1, after the fold already
works. See cacaa1c: "a pack this build would refuse to fold is a pack it must
not write."

Four new conflict types mirroring the status set: priority-rename,
priority-retired, priority-definition, priority-arity. Color disagreement folds
into priority-definition rather than getting its own type - a color lives inside
the definition, so it converges the way a label does. No new root conflict type;
nothing this build seeds a genesis with a priorities section, which is why
display added none.

Arity rules, enforced in Validate and repaired by ApplyConfig on replay: at
least one live priority, and exactly one carrying `default`.

## Ordering and defaults

  - priorityOrder() (service.go:1469) becomes a vocabulary lookup by rank.
    Call sites keep their shape: `next` selection (service.go:379) and board
    sorting (service.go:1451).
  - The hardcoded `priority = PriorityMedium` (service.go:160) becomes
    vocabulary.Default().
  - Stored values resolve rather than get rewritten. A task written as `high`
    before a rename keeps those bytes; Resolve walks the alias chain, and it
    settles the next time something writes to that task.

NO PROJECTION CHANGE. internal/projection stores priority as opaque TEXT and
does no ordering in SQL, so there is no schema change and no SQLite migration.

## Color and rendering

boardTheme composes template.CSS in Go so every byte is a property name it
wrote or an integer it parsed. Priorities extend that: for each live priority
the theme block emits --wb-priority-<name> in both schemes plus
`.priority--<name> { color: var(--wb-priority-<name>); }`. Cards already carry
data-priority. Priority names share the status name charset (lowercase,
hyphens), which is what makes them safe as class and property names.

The static stylesheet keeps built-in --wb-priority-high/medium/low, so an
unconfigured project is served no theme block and renders what it renders today.

The dark reading uses toned(hue, lightness), which keeps the chosen hue and
STATES the lightness. This doubles as a contrast clamp: the author picks the
hue, the scheme picks the lightness, so a pale yellow becomes a legible amber
in light and a lifted one in dark.

What replaces #131's triad argument: "three colors read against each other" is
not expressible at N, but the load-bearing half survives - priority colors are
still not derived from --wb-primary, so a red-ish accent still cannot make the
least urgent priority read as the most urgent. Rewrite the comment in
display.go to say that; do not delete it.

## Release policy

Raising SupportedFormatGeneration withdraws a capability from clones already in
the field: they can still fetch, read and publish their own tasks, but can no
longer change that project's configuration. That implies at least
release:minor (0.5.1 -> 0.6.0), never release:patch - which CONTRIBUTING
describes as "for a fix that does not warrant prose" and permits with no
changelog entry at all.

CONTRIBUTING currently states no patch-vs-minor policy. Add the rule there in
stage 1. v0.5.1 shipped generation 2 as a patch with no changelog mention,
which is the miss this rule prevents.

Also stale and fixed in stage 1: docs/architecture.md:249 lists only generations
0 and 1. Add the missing row for 2 and the new row for 3.

## Stages

STAGE 1 - core. PriorityVocabulary, extracted primitives, config operations,
conflict types, built-in set, generation bump (last commit), CONTRIBUTING rule,
architecture.md table. No user-visible change; the board renders identically.

STAGE 2 - cli. workbook priority <list|add|rename|relabel|remove|move|tag|untag|
recolor>, mirroring workbook status. Regenerates .workbook/guidelines.md.

STAGE 3 - board. Config-route panel, generated --wb-priority-* per project in
both schemes, .priority--<name> rules, task-detail select.

## How each stage proves itself

  1 An unconfigured project is byte-identical -> golden test against the
    previous release, written BEFORE the change (the technique v0.5.0 used for
    statuses, #82).
  1 The extraction changed no meaning -> existing vocabulary tests pass unedited.
  1 Forwarding and arity work -> mirror of the status conflict/replay suite.
  2 Commands match the status surface -> mirror of the workbook status tests.
  3 Every priority gets a dark reading -> extends #132's
    GivesEveryPalettePropertyADarkReading to generated properties.

## Cleanup carried along

Rename TestHandlerStylesheetWritesNoColourOutsideTheRootBlocks to ...Color...,
and fix the "colour" spellings introduced in #131/#132.

comments.author: a@example.com
comments.body:
Stage 1 (core) merged 2026-09-12 as PR #133 — https://github.com/dgoings/workbook/pull/133

core.Priority is now a project-configured vocabulary in the shared configuration ledger: definitions, labels, rank order, a default tag, an optional color, rename and retirement forwarding, growth ceilings, arity repair, four conflict types, and the reconcile classifiers. Nothing user-visible changed for a project holding valid history — verified by running base and HEAD binaries against one project created by the base binary.

Raises the writer-format generation to 3. Whatever release gathers this must be release:minor, per the rule the PR adds to CONTRIBUTING.md.

TWO THINGS STAGE 2 MUST HANDLE, both recorded in the PR body and in code:
1. The first priority.add on an unconfigured project would strand every existing task. Reads treat a nil section as the built-in three; the fold starts from nil as empty. One add yields a vocabulary of one while every task is still high/medium/low. A comment beside configPriorities explains why the obvious fixes are not obviously right. Stage 2 must solve this before it ships an authoring path.
2. PriorityVocabulary has no Forwarding() sibling, which is why the priority filter refuses an undefined token where the status filter reports a miss. Stage 2 wants that reporting path.

Starting stage 2 (CLI verbs) on branch feat/priority-cli.
